newsitem.title: USA: Diana's gowns to be sold for charity - Christie's.
newsitem.headline: Diana's gowns to be sold for charity - Christie's.

text.p: Stung by weeks of speculation, Christie's auction house announced on Tuesday that it will sell 80 of Princess Diana's best ballroom gowns and evening dresses to benefit cancer and AIDS charities.

Christie's said the sale in New York on June 25 would leave the princess's closets almost bare of ball gowns and "dress-up" dresses that she had used on state visits around the world. "She will have 10 left after the sale," Christie's International chairman Lord Hindlip said.

Sources at the auction house said they hoped the formal announcement would counter misleading press reports including charges Diana would profit from the sale or was staging "a bonfire of the vanities" to shed her image as a clotheshorse.

Lord Hindlip said all the proceeds from the sale would go to charities, including profits from the sale of catalogues. A special leather-bound edition of 250 will be personally signed by the princess and sold for $2,500 each.

In a rare move for a British royal, an outraged Diana started legal proceedings against the London Sunday Express for printing a report two days ago saying she stood to make more than $1 million from the sale. The paper said it had received a writ and was investigating the matter.
Peter Brown, a press spokesman for the sale, said it was believed that any papers the Express had were a forgery. "Christie's knows that all the money will go to charities."

New York auction experts predicted the sale could create the same kind of celebrity media frenzy that accompanied last April's sale of the late Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis' belongings but Hindlip refused to make the comparison himself.

"You will have to make that determination," he told a news conference in New York as he stood in front of five ballroom and evening gowns that the princess had worn on visits to Pakistan and President Reagan's White House.

The Onassis sale lasted a week and fetched more than $34 million as New Yorkers outbid each other for a chance to buy fake pearl necklaces and cocktail glasses. But Christie's said New York was chosen as the site for the sale because it is an international auction centre that will attract bidders from around the world, not because of the Onassis auction.

The auction world is just discovering the selling of haute couture dresses as a sale item. Christie's arch-rival Sotheby's will hold its first sales of haute couture dresses in April, hoping that a new market is being developed.
Media estimates have said the sale of the princess's gowns could realise more than $1.64 million, but Christie's said it was impossible to put a price on the gowns.
Hindlip said bidding would start at $5,000 but he would not predict where it would go from there. "There are no reserve prices," he said.
He also declined to say what sizes the dresses were. "They were custom-made, therefore they do not have a size," he said.

The dresses include gowns by designers Catherine Walker, Zandra Rhodes and Victor Edelstein. They include the black dress Diana wore to a party the night her ex-husband, Prince Charles, admitted in a TV interview that he had had an affair.
